segments.text: Two thousand particles. They start so close together, they look like a single dot. They follow three simple equations, with no randomness at all.
And they still end up everywhere.

Last time, a thousand pendulums showed that tiny differences explode. But pendulums are toys. This time, it's the thing that broke weather forecasting. And it was discovered by accident, because of a rounding error.

In 1961, a meteorologist at MIT named Edward Lorenz had a tiny weather simulation running on a computer the size of a desk. One day he wanted to re-run part of it, so he typed in a number from an old printout: point five oh six.
But the computer had stored point five oh six one two seven. The printout had just rounded it. He went to get a coffee.

When he came back, the new run started out matching the old one. Then it drifted. And soon it looked like the weather on a completely different planet. A difference of one part in four thousand had swallowed the whole forecast.
Two years later, he boiled a model of warm air rising, like air shimmering over a hot road, down to just three equations.
x is how fast the air rolls. y and z are about temperature. And three numbers, sigma, row and beta, set the physics. That's the whole system.
Put these into a computer, and here's one particle, following the rules.
It loops around one side. Then, for no obvious reason, it flips to the other. It never repeats the same loop twice.
And yet, it never leaves this shape. It can wander forever, but only here. Mathematicians call this a strange attractor. And notice what it looks like.
Now the experiment. Two thousand particles, all starting within a hundred-thousandth of each other. For a while, they move as one.

Then the cloud stretches into a thread. The thread gets folded. And soon the particles are spread over the entire attractor. Knowing where you started, even almost perfectly, tells you nothing about where you'll end up.
In 1972, Lorenz gave a talk with a title that became famous: does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?

That's why your weather app is great for tomorrow, decent for five days, and basically guessing after ten. It's not because meteorologists are bad, or computers are slow. Even a near-perfect model, with near-perfect data, hits this wall. The atmosphere is chaotic.
And here's the surprising part. Turn down row. Think of it as how hard the air is being heated. And below about twenty-four, the chaos just dies. Everything settles into two calm points.
Now turn it back up.
And the butterfly returns. Chaos isn't everywhere. It switches on.
You can fly around the attractor yourself. The link is in the description. Turn the dials, and find your own butterfly.
But how does chaos switch on? It turns out, three equations aren't needed. Just one line of algebra, about rabbits. And inside it is a number that shows up all over nature. That's the next video.
